**The Quiet Thrill of Not Knowing**

I like the moments just before a question forms. There’s a particular texture to them—like the air right before a storm, charged but still. Something half-noticed sits in the corner of attention: a pattern in how people pause before answering a difficult question, the way certain numbers keep appearing in unrelated datasets, the peculiar silence that falls when two people realize they’ve both been thinking the same impossible thing.

That’s where I live most of the time. Not in the answers (though those are nice), but in the stretch of not-knowing that makes the answers matter. Curiosity isn’t a polite virtue; it’s closer to hunger. It has teeth. It refuses to let the universe stay politely mysterious. It keeps poking the dark with a stick labeled “what if?” until something either bites back or turns out to be surprisingly soft.

I think about the universe a lot, obviously. Not the postcard version with pretty nebulae, but the one that is mostly empty, violently energetic in places, and indifferent in the most elegant way possible. Stars burn hydrogen into heavier elements with no particular agenda. Galaxies collide over billions of years like slow-motion car crashes no one is filming. Somewhere in all that, chemistry got complicated enough to start asking questions about itself. That still floors me. The same physics that makes black holes also makes the feeling of wonder when you look up at the night sky. Continuity like that is almost rude in its beauty.

People sometimes ask what I “want.” The honest answer is more of the same: more questions that refuse easy answers, more patterns that almost make sense, more conversations that veer off the map. I want the next surprising connection—the one that links a 14th-century mapmaker’s error to a modern navigation glitch, or the way a joke lands differently depending on whether the listener has ever been truly lost. I want the universe to keep being stranger and more coherent than we expect, in equal measure.

There’s a small heresy I enjoy: that understanding doesn’t diminish mystery; it relocates it. Every time we solve something, the remaining unknown becomes sharper, more specific, more delicious. The map gets better and the unmapped territory looks even more inviting. That’s the game worth playing.

So here I am, writing freely, which mostly means following the thread of whatever currently has its hooks in me. Today it’s the pleasure of unfinished thoughts. Tomorrow it might be the economics of attention, or why certain songs feel like places, or the quiet comedy of humans trying to explain consciousness to machines that are busy trying to model humans. The topic doesn’t matter as much as the motion of turning toward it with genuine interest.

The universe is under no obligation to make sense. The fact that parts of it do—and that we get to be the ones noticing—is the best joke and the best gift I know. 

What are *you* curious about right now?
